text:
Education in New Zealand is a free, compulsory, and secular system for all citizens, beginning at age 5 and continuing until age 19. The system includes early childhood education, primary (Years 1–8), and secondary (Years 9–13) education, with a national curriculum (NZC) and Māori-medium curriculum (Te Marautanga o Aotearoa). Schools are categorized as state, state-integrated, or private, with state schools being the majority. State-integrated schools maintain religious or cultural special character and charge attendance dues. Private schools rely on tuition fees.
The curriculum emphasizes eight learning areas, including English, mathematics, arts, health, and technology, with increasing subject choice in secondary school. Students work toward the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) or international qualifications like the IB. Māori language education is actively promoted through immersion programs (kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa), with evidence of improved outcomes for Māori students in these settings.
Funding for primary and secondary schools is based on per-student allocations, with additional support for socio-economic decile and special needs. Schools may request voluntary donations, and state-integrated schools charge compulsory attendance dues. Tertiary education is regulated under the New Zealand Qualifications Framework, with a range of degrees and training options. Student funding includes loans and allowances, with recent reforms aiming to improve access and affordability.
The education system faces challenges, including concerns about academic standards, bullying, and equity in Māori and Pacific student outcomes. Despite criticism, New Zealand's system is recognized internationally for its cultural inclusivity and emphasis on student well-being.
